Total length at puberty in Sebastes nudus has been documented at 11 centimeters [Lp = 11 centimeters], a size threshold that marks the onset of reproductive capacity in this viviparous rockfish. Data from coastal populations off northern Japan indicate that the wet weight at this developmental milestone averages approximately 16.5 grams [Wwp = approximately 16.5 grams], reflecting the substantial somatic investment required before gonadal maturation can commence. This relatively modest body size at sexual maturity, typical of smaller-bodied Sebastinae, contrasts with the species' ultimate total length, which reaches about 23.7 centimeters [Li = about 23.7 centimeters] in fully grown adults. Field surveys of older individuals suggest that the maximum adult body mass corresponding to this asymptotic length is roughly 177 grams [Wwi = roughly 177 grams], a value consistent with the slow, determinate growth pattern observed among temperate rockfishes. The transition from a juvenile of 11 centimeters to an adult of 23.7 centimeters spans several years and involves pronounced shifts in both foraging ecology and habitat use, including movement from rocky intertidal refuges to deeper subtidal zones.

Reproductive allocation in Sebastes nudus has been quantified under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a stable water temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. At a thermal regime of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], the gonadosomatic index (GSI) averaged 17.5% [GSI = 17.5%] during the peak spawning season. Interestingly, the same thermal environment that shapes reproductive investment also influences the species' overall lifespan. Longevity records from otolith-based ageing studies reveal that Sebastes nudus can persist for up to 10 years [am = up to 10 years] when maintained at 15 °C [T = 15 °C], though wild populations may exhibit somewhat shorter lifespans due to predation and fishing mortality. The protracted reproductive window afforded by this decadal lifespan allows females to produce multiple broods over successive spawning seasons.

The initial offspring mass of Sebastes nudus is remarkably low, with each newly extruded larva weighing approximately 0.000268 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.000268 grams]. This minuscule birth weight, which corresponds to a larval length of just a few millimeters, is consistent with the pelagic larval strategy common among scorpaeniform fishes. The larvae emerge from the maternal brood cavity as yolk-sac larvae that rely entirely on endogenous reserves during their first days of exogenous feeding. The transition from this lecithotrophic phase to active planktivory represents a critical bottleneck in early life history, as mortality rates are highest during the period immediately following yolk-sac resorption. Comparative data from related Sebastes species suggest that the small initial size of Sebastes nudus larvae may be partially offset by a relatively rapid growth rate during the first weeks of exogenous feeding, though this hypothesis requires further validation through controlled rearing experiments. The 0.000268 gram [Wwb = 0.000268 gram] larval mass represents one of the smallest reported values among northeastern Pacific rockfishes.

Reproductive activity in Sebastes nudus is tightly coupled to seasonal thermal cycles, with mating and parturition concentrated during the cooler months when water temperatures approach 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. Under these conditions, females produce a single brood per year, a reproductive frequency that reflects the energetic demands of viviparous gestation. The total length at puberty, measured at 11 centimeters [Lp = 11 centimeters], is reached after approximately two to three years of somatic growth, though individual variation in growth rate can shift this timing considerably. Once mature, females typically attain a wet weight at puberty of around 16.5 grams [Wwp = around 16.5 grams], a mass that must be sustained through efficient foraging on benthic crustaceans and small fishes. The gonadosomatic index of 17.5% [GSI = 17.5%] was recorded at the peak of ovarian development at a temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. Future studies should examine how interannual variation in prey availability modulates both the timing and magnitude of gonadal recrudescence in this commercially valuable rockfish.

The maximum recorded lifespan of Sebastes nudus reaches 10 years [am = 10 years] in individuals maintained under stable laboratory conditions at 15 °C [T = 15 °C], though field-caught specimens rarely exceed eight years due to natural mortality sources. This longevity, while modest compared to the century-scale lifespans of some deepwater Sebastes, is nevertheless notable for a relatively small rockfish achieving an ultimate total length of 23.7 centimeters [Li = 23.7 centimeters] and a corresponding maximum adult body mass of 177 grams [Wwi = 177 grams]. The species' growth trajectory, characterized by a gradual approach to asymptotic size, follows the typical pattern observed in temperate scorpaeniforms. Interestingly, the wet weight at puberty of 16.5 grams [Wwp = 16.5 grams] implies that reproductive investment begins when individuals have attained less than 10 percent of the asymptotic 177 gram [Wwi = 177 gram] body mass, a strategy that buffers against recruitment failure in variable environments by allowing a long reproductive lifespan.
